title: Prove the greedy choice
summary: Schedule the most non-overlapping meetings with an exchange argument, and find where greedy stops working.

scenario.briefing: The delivery desk has one meeting room and a list of requested time ranges. The current scheduler takes the earliest start, which can block two shorter meetings. Choose the greedy rule that maximizes the number of meetings, and be ready to justify it.

objectives.description: Choose the argument that justifies the greedy rule.
Distinguish problems where greedy is safe from where it is not.

hints: Sorting by start can choose a long meeting that blocks several shorter ones.
The earliest finishing meeting leaves the most room for the rest.
An exchange argument replaces the first choice in an optimal schedule without reducing its count.
Sort by end time, take the first that starts after the last end, and count.

misconceptions.description: Choosing the earliest start instead of the earliest finish.
misconceptions.testDescription: Handles a long interval that blocks two shorter ones.
misconceptions.feedback: An early start can be a long meeting. Choosing the earliest finish leaves the largest remaining window.

misconceptions.testDescription: Maximizes the count for overlapping ranges.
misconceptions.feedback: Shortest-first can still block two meetings that fit around another. Earliest finish is the exchange-proven rule.

misconceptions.description: Trusting a greedy rule because it seems locally sensible.
misconceptions.feedback: A local choice needs a proof or a counterexample search. Coin change is a classic case where greedy looks right and fails.

misconceptions.description: Believing every optimization problem needs a full DP table.
misconceptions.feedback: When the greedy choice property and optimal substructure hold, the greedy algorithm is simpler and faster. The proof is what matters.

sections.title: The choice rule decides the result
sections.body: For interval scheduling, sorting by earliest finish and taking each compatible meeting maximizes the count. Sorting by start or duration can fail because a long or early meeting blocks several better ones.

sections.title: An exchange argument
sections.body: Take an optimal schedule. Its first meeting finishes no earlier than the earliest-finishing meeting. Replace that first meeting with the earliest-finishing one; the rest still fit, so the count does not drop. Repeating the exchange proves the greedy rule.

sections.title: Greedy is a proof obligation
sections.body: A greedy algorithm is correct only when its local choice can be exchanged into an optimal solution. Coin change with denominations 1, 3, and 4 is a counterexample to largest-first. Test small cases and look for a proof before trusting a rule.

quiz.explanation: Running time does not prove correctness. The exchange argument shows the greedy choice can always be part of an optimal schedule.

steps.title: Know when greedy is safe
hints: A proof or a counterexample is the evidence.
Greedy can be simpler than a full table.
A local rule can fail on a small input.
Select exchange proofs, counterexamples, and simpler greedy when proven; reject greedy by intuition.

statements.label: An exchange argument can prove that a greedy choice belongs to some optimal solution.
A single counterexample is enough to reject a greedy rule.
A proven greedy algorithm can be simpler and faster than dynamic programming.
Local optimality alone does not guarantee global optimality.
Every optimization problem requires a full dynamic-programming table.

steps.explanation: Greedy is safe when proven. A counterexample is decisive, and local optimality by itself proves nothing.

accessibility.summary: Every control is reachable by keyboard, and the checks report text results rather than color alone.
